clue.text: Bridget Jones occasionally shows part of her bottom

definitions.note: Bottom here is the lowest end of a standing body rather than the backside the surface offers, so the definition points at the foot.

indicators.note: what happens occasionally happens every so often rather than all the time, so the letters are taken at intervals instead of in a run

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and every other letter of the twelve, running straight on over the gap between the names

explanation.surface: Bridget Jones now and then giving the world a flash of her backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternation runs on through the space between the two names, which is where it hides. The novels and the films made her the byword for that sort of mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: part of her bottom -> BIG TOE: the toes are the lowest end of a standing body, and the big one is the largest piece of it.

clue.text: I am having my picture taken before party gets very loud and mad

blocks.clueFragment: I am having my picture taken
blocks.note: the word the photographer asks for, said to pull the mouth into a smile
a do is a party, as in the office Christmas do
fortissimo, written ff on a score

explanation.surface: Someone poses for a photograph just before the party turns rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' is angry rather than insane, which is the only sense the answer has. The first six letters are what you say to a camera, not a food, and the enumeration splits one letter past the join.
explanation.definitionFit: mad -> CHEESED OFF: British for thoroughly fed up, matching mad in its everyday sense of cross rather than deranged.

clue.text: With which you might catch joke that bears fruit?

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun, and 'bears' means carries rather than grows, which is what the question mark owns up to.

blocks.note: a pun is the joke, and it leads because the two pieces describe a net for catching them
a net is the thing you catch with

explanation.surface: Some contraption for catching a joke turns out to produce fruit as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Run the pieces together and the wordplay is a net for jokes, which is why the joke ends up first. A punnet is the shallow cardboard basket British greengrocers sell strawberries in.
explanation.definitionFit: that bears fruit -> PUNNET: the small basket raspberries and strawberries are sold in, so it carries the fruit rather than growing it.

clue.text: A fool in Congress

blocks.note: taken as it stands
tit is British slang for an idiot

explanation.surface: An idiot holding a seat in the American legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter does all the work: the congress wanted is the old word for sex, not the building in Washington. Four letters split two and two is the hint that a single word has been cut in half.
explanation.definitionFit: in Congress -> AT IT: congress in its carnal sense, and at it is the coy English way of saying a couple are having sex.

clue.text: Setter, say, backed up toilet after wiping away runs

definitions.note: Setter is not a dictionary word for the stuff but a name for what it does: the agent that makes a jelly set.

indicators.note: anything backed up has been turned to face the way it came from, so the letters are read from the far end
to wipe something away is to take it off altogether, so the letter named goes and the rest closes up

blocks.note: eg is the standard shorthand for 'say', and it goes in turned round
a latrine is the barracks or campsite toilet
r is the cricket scorer's runs, and taking it out of LATRINE leaves LATINE

explanation.surface: A dog has backed up the toilet and someone is clearing the mess away.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'Setter, say' together as a dog by example is the trap; only the first word is the definition, and 'say' is two letters. R for runs comes straight off a cricket scoreboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Setter -> GELATINE: the agent stirred into a liquid to make it set, so it is the thing doing the setting.

clue.text: Perhaps Clare Balding broadcast could be authentic

indicators.note: somebody balding is losing the hair off the top, and the top of a word written down the grid is the letter it starts with
seed sown broadcast is flung wide with no say in where each piece lands, which is what happens to these letters

blocks.note: the name with the C off its top, leaving four letters to scatter

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a programme fronted by a familiar sports presenter is the genuine article.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare Balding is a BBC sports presenter, so 'broadcast' looks like her job rather than an instruction. Her surname is the instruction, and it is her first name that gets thinned.
explanation.definitionFit: authentic -> REAL: the plain word for something that is what it claims to be rather than a copy.

clue.text: Winchester for one night? I'm snuggling over blankets

definitions.note: 'For one' flags an example rather than a synonym: the American firm whose rifles carry the name is one such maker.

indicators.note: something turned over faces the other way, so this run of letters is read back the way it came
to blanket something is to lie right across it, so these words are covering what is wanted rather than building it

blocks.note: eight consecutive letters running from the end of the first word into the middle of the last, read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone spending a night in Winchester, tucked up warm under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester is an English cathedral city as well as a rifle, and the surface wants the hotel room. The letters run straight through a question mark and an apostrophe, which is what keeps them invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Winchester for one -> GUNSMITH: the Winchester Repeating Arms Company made the rifles that carry its name, one example of a firm that makes guns.

clue.text: Cutting lead, White Lotus recast key figure

indicators.note: to cut something is to lop it off, so the letter named next never reaches the answer
a show that is recast keeps its parts and fills them differently, which is how these letters are dealt out again

blocks.note: the lead of White Lotus is its first letter, and cutting it leaves nine
the title minus that lead letter, nine letters of fodder
a musical key, as in a symphony in E, joins the nine

explanation.surface: A television drama loses its star and hands the main part to somebody else.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Lotus is the HBO hotel drama, so 'recast' reads as production news. 'Key figure' looks like one phrase and is two jobs: a single letter out of music, then the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: figure -> SILHOUETTE: the outline of a person cut in black paper, a figure reduced to its shape alone.

clue.text: Aussies missing flight found in Science Museum

definitions.note: 'Aussies' stands for Australian natives of any kind rather than people, and the ones that cannot fly are birds.

indicators.note: what is found in something is already sitting there, so the letters are read off these words rather than built from them

blocks.note: four consecutive letters starting at the end of the first word and running into the second

explanation.surface: Australians who never made their plane turn up among the exhibits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing flight' works twice over: stranded at an airport in the surface, incapable of flying at all in the definition. The hiding place straddles the two words of the museum's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Aussies missing flight -> EMUS: the tall Australian bird, native to that continent and, like the ostrich, unable to leave the ground.

clue.text: Number Ten backed old Lib Dem's links with PC

indicators.note: backed means turned to face the other way, so these three letters are written from the end

blocks.note: the old anaesthetic is a number in the sense of a thing that numbs
the three letters written backwards
Vince Cable led the Liberal Democrats until 2019, and the 's supplies the last letter

explanation.surface: Downing Street gets behind a former Liberal Democrat's dealings with a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number Ten' reads as Downing Street until you split it, and the first word is the crossword's favourite false comparative: a thing that numbs. The Lib Dem is Vince Cable.
explanation.definitionFit: links with PC -> ETHERNET CABLES: the leads that plug a computer into a wired network, so they are literally its connections.

clue.text: Republican plugs rigged election claim in post online

indicators.note: to plug a gap is to stuff something into it, so this letter ends up among the others rather than beside them
a rigged ballot has had its contents rearranged to suit somebody, and these letters get the same treatment

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for the American party
anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A Republican pushing a stolen-election story in a message posted on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is American politics from first word to last, which is what makes the final two read as something typed on social media. Fourteen letters is a long way to look for a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: post online -> ELECTRONIC MAIL: the full name for email, the post as it travels down a wire instead of in a van.

clue.text: Open requires balls on tee

indicators.note: in a down entry what sits on something rests directly above it, so the piece named first takes the higher squares

blocks.note: six balls bowled from one end of a cricket pitch make an over
tee is how the letter T is spelt out

explanation.surface: The Open cannot get going until there are balls on the tee.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf owns the whole surface, and neither half of the wordplay comes from it: the balls are cricket's and the tee is only a letter said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Open -> OVERT: done in the open, with nothing concealed, as an overt threat is one made where everyone can see it.

clue.text: Taking off clothes, Richard Osman stirred drink

indicators.note: to take something off is to remove it, and what comes off is named immediately after
a stirred drink has had everything in it moved round, which is what these letters go through

blocks.note: a word's clothes are its outer letters, so the R and the D come off the first name
the first name stripped of that outer pair, five letters
the surname joins in whole, making ten letters to stir

explanation.surface: Richard Osman undressing and mixing himself something to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Osman is the British quiz-show host turned crime novelist. Only his first name is undressed, the surname going in untouched, which is the awkward bit to spot in a ten-letter jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: drink -> MARASCHINO: the sweet liqueur distilled from marasca cherries, now best known through the cherries steeped in it.

clue.text: Strategy that involves destroying terracotta?

definitions.note: The second half names a material rather than a policy: terracotta is Italian for baked earth, and the question mark admits that the pottery only answers to the words.

blocks.note: the military sense: an army in retreat burns the crops and wrecks the wells so the enemy inherits nothing
the potter's sense: clay taken from the ground and fired, which is earth that has been through the flames

explanation.surface: A plan of campaign that comes down to smashing the flowerpots.
explanation.walkthrough: Terracotta is Italian for cooked earth, which is how a garden urn ends up answering to a phrase out of the war reports. The strategy was Russia's against Napoleon and again against Hitler.
explanation.definitionFit: The retreat that burns everything useful behind it is a scorched-earth strategy, and terracotta is literally earth that has been scorched in a kiln.

clue.text: Can old companions set up and go quickly?

indicators.note: in a down entry something set up has been stood on its head, so the letters are read from the bottom of the column upwards

blocks.note: a tin is a can
the standard abbreviation
pets are the companions people keep at home

explanation.surface: Old friends stand a can upright and then make a dash for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words hide in plain sight: the can is a tin, the companions have four legs. The answer is what you say to a driver when you want a foot put down on the accelerator.
explanation.definitionFit: go quickly -> STEP ON IT: the order shouted at a driver, which means press the pedal and get a move on.

clue.text: Board member taps staff after mess ousting leader

definitions.note: The board is the chequered one rather than a company's, so the member is a piece standing on it and not a director.

indicators.note: what comes after something is reached later, so this piece drops below the letters already in place
to oust somebody is to drive them out, so the letter named goes and the rest closes up

blocks.note: British taps come marked C for cold and H for hot
the soldiers' dining room with its first letter gone
the leader of MESS is the letter it starts with, and that is the one ousted
to man a post is to staff it

explanation.surface: A director picks his people once the officers' mess has thrown out its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' is the verb here, not the workforce, and the taps are the bathroom's: hot and cold give up their letters constantly in crosswords. Boardroom language covers a chequered board.
explanation.definitionFit: Board member -> CHESSMAN: any of the pieces that stand on a chessboard, so it belongs to the board in the most literal way.

clue.text: I fret less with files organised into spreads individually

indicators.note: an organised collection has been put into a new arrangement, and these letters get exactly that

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
five more letters added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Worrying less about the paperwork once the filing has been sorted out.
explanation.walkthrough: Office nerves account for every word of the surface, and the answer belongs to botany. Fourteen letters with one small flag is the hardest kind of jumble to see.
explanation.definitionFit: spreads individually -> SELF-FERTILISES: a plant whose own pollen sets its own seed can go on reproducing with no second plant involved.

clue.text: Allege friend oddly looked like a creep

indicators.note: something done oddly is done at intervals rather than steadily, so the letters are picked every other one along the way

blocks.note: every second letter of the twelve, starting from the second

explanation.surface: Accusing a friend who had been eyeing somebody in a nasty way.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words have to be run together before the picking works, and it starts on the second letter rather than the first. 'Creep' names the man, so the definition is the look such a man gives.
explanation.definitionFit: looked like a creep -> LEERED: a leer is the sidelong, lecherous stare, the one expression the word creep is reserved for.

clue.text: One cracking grin, perhaps as happy as Larry

definitions.note: The definition is a specimen rather than a synonym, which is what 'perhaps' flags: the phrase is one of these, not a word for them.

indicators.note: to crack something is to split it open, so the letter named goes into the break

blocks.note: a grin is a smile, and it is the word that gets split
the figure one written as the Roman letter

explanation.surface: Somebody splitting their face with a grin, as cheerful as the proverbial Larry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As happy as Larry' is the British phrase for thoroughly contented, and it is offered here as a sample rather than a meaning. Nobody knows who Larry was.
explanation.definitionFit: as happy as Larry -> SIMILE: the phrase holds one thing up against another using 'as', which is precisely what the figure of speech does.

clue.text: It may help you with digital security

definitions.text: It may help you with digital security

blocks.note: read as a gadget or an app being recommended, and meant as a piece of you that came as standard
read as passwords and online banking, and meant anatomically: a digit is a finger, and the security is a grip

explanation.surface: Advice on how to keep your online accounts safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Digital belonged to fingers long before it belonged to computers, a digit being a finger or a toe. The thumb swings across to meet them, and that is what lets a hand hold anything at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The thumb that can swing across to meet the fingers is what gives a hand its grip, so it keeps the digits' hold secure in the literal sense.

clue.text: Quince takes job on retirement, stressful work

definitions.note: Stressful is meant literally, full of stresses, and work means a composition, so the pair describes the thing rather than the trouble of writing it.

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw, to go back the way you came, so the letters in front of it are written in reverse

blocks.note: Quince is the setter of this puzzle, so the name stands for me
an op is a job of work, as in a military op

explanation.surface: A pensioner takes on a job that turns out to be a strain.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter signing his own clue is the joke: Quince is the byline over this puzzle. Verse is measured out in stressed and unstressed syllables, which is the sense of 'stressful' being used.
explanation.definitionFit: stressful work -> POEM: verse is built from stressed and unstressed syllables, so it is a composition genuinely full of stresses.

clue.text: Maybe onion on the counter makes you cry

indicators.note: read as a kitchen worktop, but counter means running the opposite way, so the letters are taken from the far end

blocks.note: an onion is one kind of bulb, which is what maybe allows for

explanation.surface: An onion sits on the kitchen worktop waiting to bring tears to your eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture is complete and entirely false: no worktop is involved, only the direction of travel. Gardeners and cooks use the same word for what an onion is.
explanation.definitionFit: cry -> BLUB: informal British for weeping noisily, the word used of a child or of a grown-up in floods.

clue.text: The man goes round a square in Rome where it's busy

indicators.note: what goes round something encircles it, so this word opens up and the other sits inside

blocks.note: he is the man, and the two letters part to take the others in
four is a square number, and Rome wrote four as IV

explanation.surface: A man strolls round a Roman piazza on a crowded afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The square in Rome is a number and not a piazza: four is a square, and IV is the Roman way of writing it. The definition rests on bees being the proverbially busy ones.
explanation.definitionFit: where it's busy -> HIVE: the bees' home, and a hive of activity is the stock phrase for anywhere humming with work.

clue.text: Something in Tinder pictures is not quite right?

definitions.note: The first half only defines the answer once its ten letters are redivided into three words, and the second is a joke on the geometry rather than a synonym, which is what the question mark is for.

blocks.note: redivided, the first five letters become two words, and what they name is the flattering tilt people hold the phone at for a dating profile
the geometer's reading: an angle short of the ninety degrees that would make it a right one

explanation.surface: A dating profile photograph that looks a little too good to be honest.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration hides the joke: read the other way, the five letters before the gap are an article and an adjective. 'Right' is the geometer's right angle of ninety degrees, and anything under that qualifies.
explanation.definitionFit: An angle of less than ninety degrees is literally not quite a right angle, and the same letters redivided name the becoming tilt a phone camera is held at.
